# Research: the drawer wall's workflow and stack (Nov 6 2026)

A research pass made for the founder on Nov 6 2026, kept here as the reasoning behind `docs/build/DRAWER-WALL.md`. It was written for a studio budget; the run departs from it where the founder chose to build in-house at no added cost (`00-decisions.md` #45). Where they differ, `DRAWER-WALL.md` wins:

| The research says | The run does | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Scan the real calfskin (paid service), Megascans for lookdev | A procedural calfskin in Blender, world-space grain | #45: no paid services; a scan can replace it later (`launch.md`) |
| A calibrated reference and hands shoot, focus-stacked deep zoom | The cleaned lightbox set for the zoom and as the reference | #8 and O17: no reshoot unless the founder changes it |
| `WebGPURenderer` with WebGL 2 fallback, drei `<View>` | WebGL 2, one `<Canvas>` for the one lifted frame | Fewer moving parts; only one live 3D object ever exists |
| KTX2 textures | WebP textures (`EXT_texture_webp`), KTX2 later if needed | No extra binary in the toolchain |
| OpenSeadragon deep-zoom tiles | One full-resolution image per angle | Files at these sizes need no tiles; tiles later if older iPhones run short |
| Microsoft Clarity, Maze, Lookback | A local event log and five people on their own phones | No third-party scripts; no paid tools |
| Fields such as `drop_start`, `sequence_set`, `glb`, `emblem_verified` on the metaobject | Drop times stay on the drop; assets resolve through the manifest; checks run in the build | One source of truth per fact |

---

# Darkest Shades "Drawer Bay Wall" PLP: Production Workflow and Technology Stack Plan

**Recommendation: build a hybrid.** Make the wall and the eight drawers photoreal by rendering them offline (Blender Cycles, finished in compositing the way FOOH studios work) and serve them as lightweight image sequences. Bring in one real-time 3D pair of glasses (three.js / react-three-fiber, glTF + KTX2) only when a shopper lifts a frame. Back that model with real, focus-stacked photographs for deep zoom. Gaussian splatting and a physical drawer-wall build are not the right primary path for this product today. The founder's "slide finger up/down to open" mechanic will fight page scroll, so redesign it as tap-to-open with optional drag inside a focused, scroll-locked state.

## TL;DR

- **Stack:** Use pre-rendered Cycles plates and drawer sequences for the wall (FOOH-grade realism at roughly zero GPU cost). Use one shared WebGL/WebGPU canvas (three.js `WebGPURenderer` with automatic WebGL 2 fallback, plus drei `<View>`) for the single lifted pair. Use real high-res photo stacks for deep zoom. Drive each drawer from a Shopify metaobject ("drawer_bay") that the Hydrogen loader reads alongside live product inventory.
- **Interaction:** Vertical drag-to-open on a vertically scrolling grid is the critical flaw. Tap the knob to open (spring animation). Then enter a focused, scroll-locked "drawer mode" where drag, spin and pinch are safe. Every drag must have a tap/button alternative to meet WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7. Don't rely on haptics: iOS Safari has never shipped the Vibration API.
- **Captures and cost:** Required work is a calibrated reference and hands photo shoot of all 8 frames, focus-stacked deep-zoom stills, CAD-accurate 3D frames refined against those photos (lenses modeled, not scanned), and a scan of the real calfskin swatch. Plan roughly 12–16 weeks. Rough external spend is low five figures for assets plus WebGL development time. Ink N Algorithm's 2026 eyewear configurator guide quotes $500–$2,000 per frame (3–7 days) for 3D models, and 360° photography runs $100–$500 per product.

## Key Findings

### 1. What "FOOH-level" realism actually comes from

FOOH studios have no single magic engine. Maverick Frame, in its "What Is FOOH?" explainer, says "there's no single 'FOOH program.' It's a task, and the tools follow. We model in 3ds Max, build effects in Houdini, composite in Nuke or After Effects", adding that "more and more of it gets done with AI." Others describe a "Houdini → Unreal → Nuke pipeline", or modeling in Cinema 4D/Houdini with rendering in Redshift and Octane. The common thread is matching camera and lighting, then compositing. FOOH is CGI combined with real footage, where "camera tracking locks the CGI to the real footage… lighting and shadows are matched so the object sits in the world."

**What this means for Darkest Shades:** the realism bar is set by lookdev, lighting and the final grade (lens, depth of field, halation, grain), not by a real-time engine. The founder already has Cycles, which is a production path tracer. The quality jump comes from three things:
- real material data (scanned leather, measured frames);
- photographic lighting reference;
- a compositing pass (grain, lens softness, a near-black grade) applied identically to every frame.

I could not open the FOOH page for the reference film directly (access was blocked). The tone brief here therefore relies on the founder's description: near-black, soft cinematic light, shallow focus, grain, intimate.

### 2. Comparing realism approaches for the drawers and wall

| Approach | Realism | Mobile GPU / battery | Load | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Pre-rendered offline (Cycles/Octane/Redshift) sequences or video scrub | Highest; full path tracing, true soft shadows, leather sheen | Near zero (image decode only) | Moderate; must budget frames | Low–medium (render time + artist) | **Primary for wall and drawers** |
| (b) Real-time WebGL/WebGPU PBR with baked lightmaps and HDRI | High for hard surfaces; leather micro-sheen and soft contact shadows usually fall short of path-traced | Highest, especially with 8 live instances | Large GLBs, shader compile | Medium–high dev | Use only for the one lifted pair |
| (c) Hybrid (baked plates + real-time hero) | Highest *where it matters* | Low (one live 3D object max) | Best balance | Medium | **Recommended overall** |
| (d) Gaussian splat / NeRF of real objects | Excellent for matte, diffuse objects; weak on glossy black acetate and dark lenses (see §4) | Moderate–high (sorting) | Splat files are heavy | Low capture cost, high cleanup | R&D only |
| (e) Photograph a real built drawer wall | Real by definition | Same as (a) | Same as (a) | Prop build + shoot; inflexible for per-drawer states and new drops | Viable alternative to CGI for the *wall*; loses flexibility |
| Unreal/Unity pixel streaming | Very high | Offloaded to a cloud GPU | Video stream; latency | Ongoing per-session GPU server cost | Not justified for a PLP |

The drawers are **identical**, which is what makes (a)/(c) cheap. Render one drawer-open sequence once, with separate passes (drawer, interior shadow, emblem knob). Then composite each product's glasses into the open-drawer frames, or render a short per-product "glasses in tray" layer. Lighting variants per drawer (lamp on/off, dimmed for sold-out) are extra render passes or CSS-blended layers, not new 3D scenes.

On engine choice for the real-time part: three.js now ships `WebGPURenderer`, and "browsers without WebGPU get the WebGL 2 fallback". Safari has shipped WebGPU "since v26 (September 2025) on macOS, iOS, iPadOS, and visionOS." Babylon.js, PlayCanvas and Needle are credible alternatives. three.js/r3f fits a React/Remix Hydrogen codebase most naturally and has the largest ecosystem (drei, gltf-transform, Spark for splats).

### 3. Leather: what real material capture is needed

- **Buy and scan the actual calfskin with its piping.** Vizoo xTex captures an A4 swatch "in 1 – 3 minutes… at 600 dpi" and accepts "fabric, synthetic, leather, metal" with PBR outputs: base color, roughness, metalness, normal, displacement. Binarycloth's pricing page lists "Vizoo scanning: Start From $30… MOQ: 15 Pieces", so its real minimum spend is about $450. Bandicoot Imaging offers "$30 USD per fabric face" or a "$125 USD for 5 fabrics" pilot. A 2021 review cited €19 per material as a service. X-Rite TAC7 (AxF) is the high-end option, but its AxF materials are noted as GPU-heavy for real-time use, and it is overkill here.
- **Base library:** As of November 5, 2026, Quixel announced "the full Quixel Megascans library free on Fab", and Fab's leather category includes top-grain and full-grain black leathers. Use these as a starting point and for lookdev tests. Final renders should use the scanned swatch so the brand's leather is honest.
- **Authoring:** Substance 3D Sampler turns photos into tileable PBR materials. The Texturing plan is $24.99/month after Adobe's March 2025 price rise. Blender's free procedural tools are enough for wear, piping and edge-paint detail.
- **Lighting for the mood:** one large, heavily diffused key from high three-quarter, a dim negative-fill environment, and a narrow rim/top light to trace the piped edges. Add a warm practical inside the drawer that blooms when it opens. Capture an HDRI of the real photo set during the reference shoot, so the CG lighting and the real photographs share one light (this is the FOOH "match the lighting" principle).

### 4. The glasses: true look, free spin, deep zoom

**Hard truth: no single technology gives free 3D rotation *and* infinite, lossless, provably real zoom.** A real-time model can rotate freely, but its "truth" is only as good as its lookdev. A photograph is true, but only from the angle where it was shot. The honest answer is a hybrid: real-time 3D for spin, real photographs for zoom and for the hero "in hand" moment.

**Option comparison:**

- **(a) CAD/drawing-based 3D model (recommended base).** The founder already has 1:1 technical drawings and a procedural Blender model. That is the most dimensionally accurate start, better than photogrammetry for thin temples and hinges. Refine it against calibrated photos and export glTF/GLB. Material extensions to use:
  - Lenses: `KHR_materials_transmission` + `KHR_materials_volume`. Transmission "more accurately represents refractive materials like glass", and volume adds "refraction and absorption" (tint via attenuationColor/Distance).
  - Glossy acetate: clearcoat.
  - Iridescence: only if a lens is actually mirrored.
  - Anisotropy: only for brushed metal hinges. Khronos describes it as giving "the visually distinct feature of an elongated appearance of the specular reflection."

  Caveat: JS renderers "cannot combine multiple layers of transmissive objects," so test lens-over-lens views.
- **(b) 360° multi-row turntable photography.** This is truthful but discrete (you can only show captured angles), heavy for deep zoom, and black glossy eyewear is a premium job. 360 Product Video (360productvideo.com) charges $59 down to $33 per photo, but says that rate "does not include special items such as sunglasses, reflective items, and large items." Market pricing runs $100–$500 per product (multi-row "$350–$500+"). Precision Studios in Los Angeles (mylaphotographer.com) lists $90/$150/$250/$350 for 12/24/36/72-frame spins. Use it for authenticity, not as the main spin engine.
- **(c) Gaussian splatting.** The web tooling is mature. Spark (World Labs, MIT) runs on "98%+ WebGL2" devices and streams LoD. three.js is gaining native SPZ/`KHR_gaussian_splatting` support. The physics is the problem:
  - Vanilla 3DGS colour uses spherical harmonics, "inherently limited to low-frequency view-dependent effects and thus inadequate for representing the high-frequency reflections."
  - Chen & Wang's "A Survey on 3D Gaussian Splatting" (ACM Computing Surveys 58(12), Art. 313, published 15 May 2026) states "robust reconstruction of reflective and transparent objects in general scenes remains challenging."
  - The newest research methods (RT-GS, RT-Splatting) handle only thin semi-transparent surfaces and do "not explicitly model refraction."

  Glossy black acetate plus dark tinted lenses is close to a worst case. Splats also bake in the capture lighting, so they won't sit in the moody drawer light, and zooming past capture resolution turns them into blobs. **Run it as an R&D test only.**
- **(d) Neural or relightable assets.** These are research-grade (e.g., TransparentGS, SIGGRAPH 2025). They are not production-ready for an e-commerce launch.
- **(e) Hybrid (recommended).** Real-time GLB for spin plus small zoom (around 2–3×). At deeper zoom, or on a "See real photo" tap, cross-fade to a matched-angle, focus-stacked real photograph served as deep-zoom tiles (OpenSeadragon/IIIF). Zoom resolution is then bounded by real photographic data, not texture size, and the shopper always ends on the truth.

**Capture prep for black acetate and dark lenses:**
- **For geometry only:** AESUB Transparent is a "self-vanishing dulling spray" (15–20 µm layer, sublimates in up to about 4 hours) for photogrammetry. It mattes glossy acetate so it can be scanned or verified against CAD.
- **Never on lenses in a way that risks coatings.** Confirm with the lens supplier first.
- **Never in final beauty photos.**
- **For appearance:** use cross-polarized plus parallel-polarized pairs to separate diffuse colour from specular, and focus-stack the macro detail.
- **Authenticity rule:** sprayed captures are only a geometry source. Every appearance and colour judgment must be checked against unsprayed reference photos taken under a ColorChecker.

**Model-sourcing costs:**
- Ink N Algorithm's 2026 eyewear configurator guide quotes "3D model per frame $500–$2,000, 3–7 days", and "AR try-on (single frame, basic) $8,000–$25,000" in the same table.
- Fittingbox digitizes frames at "€9 to €250 per frame depending on the level of quality."
- AI photo-to-3D tools advertise minutes per model, but they are vendor marketing and unlikely to meet a FOOH bar or 1:1 accuracy.

Because the CAD-based Blender models already exist, the main spend is lookdev and optimization, not modeling from scratch.

### 5. Mobile touch interaction: evaluating the proposed mechanic

**Research grounding:**
- Steven Hoober's 2013 UXmatters study, "How Do Users Really Hold Mobile Devices?", observed 1,333 people, 780 of whom were touching the screen. Of those, 49% held the phone one-handed, 36% cradled it, and 15% used two hands.
- His later work (millions of touches) found that people "prefer to view and touch the center of the screen", and that targets can be "as small as 7 millimeters" in the centre but about 12 mm in the corners.
- He now calls fixed thumb-zone charts "well-known, but incorrect" because grips shift constantly.

**Implications:** put the lifted glasses and primary controls in the centre band, and put secondary actions (Add to bag, close) along the bottom edge.

**The scroll conflict is the critical problem.** On a vertically scrolling grid, a vertical drag on a drawer is ambiguous: the browser must decide between scrolling and your gesture *at touch start*. You "can't change `touch-action` after the `pointerdown`," so you can't decide later. If you set `touch-action: none` on drawer faces that fill the screen, users can't scroll the page. Pull-to-refresh and iOS edge-swipe-back add more conflicts.

**Recommended mechanics:**

1. **Grid state:** drawers keep `touch-action: pan-y`, so page scroll is always native. **Tap** a drawer (or its knob, with a target of at least 24×24 CSS px under WCAG 2.5.8 and ideally 44 px+) to open it with a spring animation scrubbing the pre-rendered sequence. The drawer face can also show a subtle 2–3 frame "breathing" pull on first view as an affordance hint.
2. **Focused "drawer mode":** the opened drawer animates to the centre and the page scroll locks (`overscroll-behavior: contain`, with `touch-action: none` on the stage only). Here a vertical drag *can* scrub the drawer in and out with inertia and springs, because there is no competing scroll. Close with a visible button, tap outside, or drag down.
3. **Lift:** tap the glasses, not "pull them toward you". Pulling toward the viewer has no on-screen direction, so the cue is not discoverable. Use the label "Tap to lift" and keep "pull" only as brand copy. The lifted pair enters a centred, lit close-up.
4. **Inspect:** one-finger drag spins (horizontal = yaw, damped vertical = limited pitch). Pinch or double-tap zooms. Add visible ⟲ ⟳ / + − buttons and a "View real photos" button to satisfy SC 2.5.1 (path and multipoint gestures need single-pointer alternatives) and SC 2.5.7 ("for any action that involves dragging, provide a simple pointer alternative"). A swipe alone does not qualify as that alternative.
5. **Put back:** tap "Put back" or tap the drawer. Don't rely on a drag.
6. **Tap vs drag threshold:** treat movement under about 8–10 px as a tap. A typical gesture library default is `threshold: 10`. Use pointer events with `pointercancel` handling.
7. **Haptics:** Android Chrome supports `navigator.vibrate`. "Safari has never implemented the Vibration API". The `<input type=checkbox switch>` workaround is fragile, and since iOS 26.5 reportedly "only the user's own tap on it plays that tick." Treat haptics as Android-only polish and never the sole feedback.
8. **Reduced motion:** under `prefers-reduced-motion`, swap the scrub for a cross-fade and turn off auto-tilt and parallax. Keep the gyroscope or CSS tilt opt-in.
9. **Screen readers and keyboard:** each drawer is a real `<button>` with an accessible name (frame name, price, state "sold out / opens Fri 18:00"). The 3D view has a text description and a link to the standard product photos.

**Usability testing plan:**
- Run 5–8 moderated remote sessions on the participants' own phones (Lookback or similar) before building in code, using a clickable prototype of the prerendered frames.
- Follow with unmoderated mobile tests (Maze/UserTesting) for first-click and task success: "find a frame that's in stock and see it up close".
- After launch, use session replay and heatmaps (e.g., Microsoft Clarity, which is free) and A/B test drag-first against tap-first.

**Metrics to track:**
- drawer-open rate per session, and time-to-first-open;
- mis-scroll rate (scroll starts on a drawer then reverses);
- lift rate, and spin/zoom engagement;
- "View real photos" usage;
- add-to-bag from the drawer;
- rage taps;
- INP on real devices;
- bounce relative to a plain grid control.

### 6. Per-drawer architecture (Shopify Hydrogen)

**Data model (Shopify-native, no extra CMS needed):**
- Metaobject `drawer_bay`, with storefront access enabled. The Storefront API requires the `unauthenticated_read_metaobjects` scope. Fields:
  - `position` (int) and `product` (product reference);
  - `state` (enum: available / locked / coming_soon / sold_out / hidden);
  - `drop_start` and `drop_end` (datetime);
  - `lighting_preset` (enum);
  - `sequence_set` (file/JSON reference);
  - `glb` (file or product 3D media);
  - `deepzoom_manifest` (URL);
  - `emblem_verified` (boolean QA flag).
- Metaobject `bay_wall` holds an ordered list of `drawer_bay` references, so drag-reorder in Shopify admin sets the grid order.
- Inventory and sell-out stay authoritative on the Product/Variant (`availableForSale`, quantity), not duplicated in the metaobject.

**Server logic:** the Remix loader merges the metaobject state, live availability and drop time on the server, so a drawer can't be "opened early" by client clock tampering. Cache metaobjects briefly; never cache inventory long.

**Component model:**
- `<BayWall>` maps to N `<DrawerBay>` components. Each is a self-contained React component with its own state machine (idle → opening → open → lifted → inspecting → closing, plus locked/sold-out branches), its own sequence preloader, and its own analytics events.
- All rendering of drawer motion is image-based, so 8, 16 or 40 drawers cost about the same as one.
- **Exactly one real-time 3D instance** exists at a time. A single shared `<Canvas>` uses drei `<View>`, which uses "gl.scissor to cut the viewport into segments… multiple views with a single, performant canvas."
- Don't create a canvas per drawer. Multiple canvases "take resources… you can't share data between them, the browser will kill them if you have an arbitrary amount of them."
- Lazy-load the three.js chunk and the GLB only on the first "lift" intent (prefetch on drawer open). Before that, the page ships no WebGL.

**Progressive enhancement and fallback tiers:**
- **Tier 0:** no JS / Save-Data / very low memory. A static poster grid of real photos with standard product links.
- **Tier 1:** image sequences plus real photo zoom.
- **Tier 2:** add the real-time lifted 3D.

Choose the tier from `navigator.deviceMemory`, `hardwareConcurrency`, a WebGL/WebGPU probe and Save-Data, and allow a manual "Lite mode" toggle.

### 7. Performance budgets (mobile, 390 px first)

| Item | Budget | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Core Web Vitals | LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 at p75 | Google web.dev thresholds |
| LCP element | A single pre-rendered wall poster (AVIF, ~120–200 KB at 390 px), not a canvas | Recommendation |
| Initial page transfer (above-fold) | ≤ ~1 MB including JS; no three.js in the initial bundle | Recommendation |
| Drawer sequence | 11–24 frames × ~25–40 KB AVIF/WebP per drawer at 2× DPR (≈0.3–1 MB), loaded on viewport proximity | Recommendation |
| Glasses GLB | ~2–4 MB target; ≤ 15 MB hard ceiling | Shopify: "approximately 4 MB… must not exceed 15 MB" |
| Triangles (glasses) | 30–50k ideal; ≤ 100k | Google Scene Viewer guidance |
| Textures | ≤ 2048² per map; KTX2 (UASTC for normals/ORM, ETC1S for color) | Scene Viewer max; KTX2 stays compressed on GPU |
| Draw calls | ≤ 15 for the hero object (ideally a few merged materials); scene < 100 | Google DV360 3D: "15 or less… ideally 1"; three.js rule of thumb "<100 draw calls" |
| Geometry compression | Meshopt or Draco via gltf-transform | Standard practice |

On texture memory: a Khronos blog post on KTX 2.0 in OGC I3S v1.2 states that "KTX 2.0 textures in GPU memory are 6-8X smaller than JPEG textures." Paradowski Creative's ZenCompress post cites a similar "4–8x reduction in memory use", so verify either figure on your own assets.

Render the real-time canvas on demand (`frameloop="demand"`), so the GPU idles when the user isn't touching it. That protects battery life.

### 8. Brand and honesty constraints

- **GCD emblem:** model it as a locked, separate mesh and material, built from caliper measurements and macro photos of the physical hardware. Its transform is constrained relative to the frame's hinge/temple datum and is never re-scaled per render. Add an `emblem_verified` QA gate per asset: overlay the render against a reference photo at a fixed camera, with a tolerance check. Every pre-rendered sequence, GLB and photo is signed off with the emblem visible at its true size and placement.
- **Honest product appearance:**
  - Lens tint, acetate colour and gloss must be matched to ColorChecker-calibrated reference photos.
  - The deep-zoom view is always real photography.
  - The "in human hands" hero should be **real photographs/video of real hands** in the drawer lighting, not AI-generated people. Existing AI cast images with composited frames can stay as lifestyle or mood material, clearly not used as the product-truth view. Consider labeling them as such.
  - No invented specs. Dimensions shown come from the technical drawings.

## Recommended Stack

- **DCC / render:** Blender (Cycles) for modeling, lookdev and offline renders; compositing in Blender or Nuke/DaVinci Fusion for grain and grade. Houdini is optional and not needed for this scope.
- **Materials:** a Vizoo-scanned calfskin swatch; Megascans (free on Fab) for lookdev; Substance 3D Sampler/Painter for the acetate and emblem.
- **Web:** Hydrogen (Remix) + React; three.js `WebGPURenderer` (WebGL 2 fallback) via react-three-fiber and drei `<View>`; @use-gesture plus react-spring/motion for springs; gltf-transform (KTX2 + meshopt) for the asset pipeline; OpenSeadragon for deep-zoom tiles; Spark kept in reserve for splat R&D.
- **Backend control:** Shopify metaobjects + product inventory; no separate headless CMS unless editorial needs grow.
- **Testing:** BrowserStack or a physical device lab (at least an iPhone SE/older iPhone, a mid-range Android and a flagship of each), WebPageTest, the web-vitals RUM library, Microsoft Clarity, and Maze/Lookback for UX research.

## Workflow / Pipeline

| Phase | Weeks | Outputs | Roles |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Pre-production | 1–2 | Interaction prototype (Figma/ProtoPie using existing renders), tone boards, shot list, data model, budgets | Founder, UX lead, WebGL lead |
| 1. Capture | 2–4 | Reference/hands shoot of all 8 frames + HDRI + ColorChecker; focus-stacked deep-zoom stills; emblem macro + measurements; calfskin scan | Product photographer, 3D lead |
| 2. Modeling & lookdev | 3–8 | CAD-accurate frames refined vs photos; acetate/lens materials; drawer + wall lookdev | 3D artist, lookdev/lighting artist |
| 3. Lighting & offline render | 6–9 | Wall plate, drawer sequences (states/lighting variants), per-product tray layers, final grade | Lighting/comp artist |
| 4. Real-time asset prep | 7–10 | GLBs (KTX2, meshopt, budgets met), matched-angle photo set for cross-fade | Technical artist |
| 5. Web integration | 6–12 | DrawerBay components, state machines, metaobject wiring, lazy loading, fallback tiers | WebGL/front-end developer |
| 6. QA on real phones | 11–13 | Performance traces, battery/thermal checks, a11y audit (WCAG 2.2 AA), emblem/honesty sign-off | Developer, QA, accessibility reviewer |
| 7. Usability testing | 2–3 (prototype), 12–14 (build) | Moderated + unmoderated results, iteration | UX researcher |
| 8. Launch & measure | 14–16 | RUM dashboards, replay/heatmap review, A/B test | Founder, UX, dev |

**Asset management:** keep versioned source files (.blend, scans, raws) in cloud storage with a naming scheme (`frame-slug_asset_version`). Serve published web assets from Shopify Files/CDN or an image CDN, referenced by metaobject fields, so a new drop is a data change, not a deploy.

## What the Founder Must Provide

- All 8 physical frames (production samples, with the actual lenses), plus spares if possible for spray and scan work.
- The 1:1 technical drawings, measurements and lens specs (tint, category, polarization), so nothing is invented.
- The physical GCD emblem hardware (or one loose piece), with its exact size and placement spec.
- A physical calfskin swatch with piping, from the actual supplier.
- The existing Blender files, the 11-frame prototype, lightbox photos, and the AI cast images (to triage).

## Rough Costs and Timeline (planning ranges)

| Item | Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Reference + hands + deep-zoom photo shoot (8 frames, 1–2 days) | ~$2k–$6k | Estimate; black glossy eyewear is priced above standard product rates |
| 360° multi-row spins (optional) | $100–$500+/frame → ~$0.8k–$4k | Market ranges cited above |
| 3D frame refinement/lookdev | $500–$2,000/frame → $4k–$16k (less if in-house models hold up) | Ink N Algorithm configurator pricing |
| Leather scan | $30 per material face (Bandicoot Imaging; $125 for a 5-fabric pilot); Binarycloth $30 with a 15-piece minimum (~$450) | Vizoo service pricing |
| Megascans / Substance | $0 / $24.99 per month | Free on Fab since Nov 2026; Adobe Texturing plan |
| Drawer/wall lookdev + renders | ~$3k–$10k freelance, or founder time | Estimate |
| WebGL/front-end build | ~4–8 developer-weeks | Estimate; the main cost driver |
| UX research tools/participants | Low hundreds to low thousands | Estimate |

Overall timeline is about 12–16 weeks to a tested launch. The cost estimates above are my planning assumptions where no source is cited. Get 2–3 quotes for each.

## Caveats

- Several sources are vendor or agency blogs; I flagged their numbers where relevant. The KTX2 memory figures (Khronos blog 6–8× vs JPEG; Paradowski 4–8×) should be verified on your own assets, and the "<100 draw calls" rule is secondary.
- Gaussian-splat research is moving fast (2025–2026 papers). Re-check in 6–12 months; it may become viable for the acetate frames, but probably still not for dark lenses.
- WebGPU on iOS requires iOS 26+. Older devices fall back to WebGL 2, so test both paths.
- The iOS haptic workaround is undocumented behaviour and may change.
